newsitem.title: USA: Use less stuff -- ecologically sound shopping.
newsitem.headline: Use less stuff -- ecologically sound shopping.

text.p: Stuff abhors a vacuum. In other words, the more space you have, the more stuff you can use to fill it. Right?

Wrong says The USL Report, a consumer shopping newsletter from Ann Arbor, Mich., dedicated to the proposition that the less stuff you have, the less stuff you use, the better off we'll all be -- not only this generation but ones down the road.
The 3-year-old bi-monthly newsletter advocates consumer-friendly "source reduction" -- the all-around use of less stuff.

Source reduction can come in the form of less packaging, concentrated products, energy conservation, reuse of materials and the purchase of long-lasting and repairable appliances. It results in less waste and lower costs for consumers.
While recycling materials is important, it's not the entire picture. The ULS Report also advocates planning so that there is less all-around waste or spoilage.
Articles in the four-page newsletter offer consumers guidance in reducing waste as they shop in the local grocery store or mall.
Much of source reduction can come from individuals, for example, who can pack groceries in cloth tote bags rather than bags from the stores.
But on a large scale, source reduction can come from corporations. One example is the trend toward concentrated products.
These products, such as dish detergent or cleaning solutions, do the same amount of work as larger amounts, but use far less packaging, producing less waste or less to be recycled.

"The word is out," said Lisa Morgan, a spokeswoman for the newsletter. "Source reduction goes further than just recycling. But unfortunately, you can't really legislate source reduction," she said from New York.
Government, corporate and individual moves toward source reduction are "getting the message across, but it's not easy.
"It's easier to see papers piled up and know they are being recycled. It's harder to be proactive and reduce the amount of stuff," Morgan said.

The ULS Report is edited by Robert Lilienfeld in Ann Arbor, Mich., where he is the president of The Cygnus Group, which consults with organisations on how to integrate environmental concepts into long term strategic planning and marketing.
The report also uses the services of Dr. William Rathje of the University of Arizona, an archaeologist who studies the contents of landfills.
Recently, The ULS Report listed its 1997 honour roll, highlighting mainstream companies and products that are taking the lead by using less stuff.

Honourees include Quaker Oats Co. for its bagged cereals, which reduce waste by 85 percent and bring the price down by almost half; Procter & Gamble for its concentrated cleaners, which save millions of pounds of plastic from going to the trash and reduce the price per wash; and Planters, which is now using flexible pouches for its snacks, reducing waste by 75 percent.

PepsiCo, which substituted reusable plastic cases for one-way shippers, saved itself $44 million annually, and also saved the environment by not needing 196 million pounds of corrugated materials each year, The ULS Report stated.
By using less stuff, consumers also win. Part of the theory behind source management requires smart shopping and, thus, saves money.
"If you shop smart and are inventive with what you already have," there can be tremendous savings because of less waste, Morgan said.
The ULS Top 10 shopping list suggests:
1. Buy concentrates, refills and flexible packaging.
2. Purchase products that come in packages that contain post consumer recycled (PCR) materials.
3. Reuse packaging as much as possible, especially paper and plastic bags, glass containers etc.
4. Buy multiple-use products, such as detergents with bleach or fabric softener, shampoos with conditioner or items that perform more than one function.
5. Buy in bulk whenever practical.
6. Buy appliances and electronic products that are durable, long-lasting and repairable.
7. Plan shopping and errands ahead of time, using fewer car trips.
8. Buy only what can be eaten before spoiling.
9. Buy produce without extra packaging.
10. Borrow or rent items that you may use only for a short time or infrequently.
